title: Bellarmine quoted: opponents call rectitude natural like health; Rome calls it supernatural in itself, so fallen man differs from pure-natural man as the stripped from the naked
source_text: XI. Adversarii, inquit, censent rectitudinem illam in qua creatus est Adam fuisse illi naturalem hoc ultimo modo (nempe quatenus naturale opponitur supernaturali) nimirum quod fuerit veluti quaedam sanitas debita naturae, aptaque nasci ex ipsa natura bene constituta, id est, non corrupta: & nunc hominibus qui eam rectitudinem amiserunt in Adamo, deesse bonum aliquod naturale, quale deesse pecudi, si caeca, vel claudicans, vel febricitans nasceretur. Et nunc, si alicui homini originalis illa justitia divinitus redderetur, dicerent esse donum supernaturale per accidens, non per se, ut diximus de oculis redditis caeco nato. Nos vero existimamus rectitudinem illam, etiam partis inferioris, fuisse donum supernaturale, & quidem per se, non per accidens, ita ut neque ex principiis naturae fluxerit, neque potuerit fluere. Et quia donum illud supernaturale erat, ut statim probaturi sumus, eo remoto, natura humana sibi relicta pugnam illam experiri coepit partis inferioris cum superiore, quae naturalis futura erat, id est, ex conditione materiae sequutura, nisi Deus justitiae donum homini addidisset. Quare non magis differt status hominis post lapsum Adae, a statu ejusdem in puris naturalibus, quam differt spoliatus a nudo: neque deterior est humana natura, si culpam originalem detrahas, neque magis ignorantia & infirmitate laborat, quam esset & laboraret in puris naturalibus condita. Proinde corruptio naturae non ex alicujus doni naturalis carentia, neque ex alicujus malae qualitatis accessu, sed ex sola doni supernaturalis ob Adae peccatum amissione profluxit. Quam sententiam communem esse Doctorum Scholasticorum veterum & recentiorum, multis postea allatis eorum testimoniis probat.
pass_a_gloss: The Adversaries, he says, think that that rectitude in which Adam was created was natural to him in this last way (namely insofar as natural is opposed to supernatural) namely because it was as it were a certain health owed to nature, and apt to be born from nature itself well constituted, that is, not corrupt: and now to men who lost that rectitude in Adam, some natural good is lacking, such as would be lacking to a beast, if it were born blind, or lame, or feverish. And now, if that original justice were divinely restored to some man, they would say it is a supernatural gift per accidens, not per se, as we said of eyes restored to the man born blind. But we think that that rectitude, even of the lower part, was a supernatural gift, and indeed per se, not per accidens, so that it neither flowed from the principles of nature, nor could flow. And because that gift was supernatural, as we shall prove at once, when it was removed, human nature left to itself began to experience that fight of the lower part with the higher, which was going to be natural, that is, to follow from the condition of matter, unless God had added the gift of justice to man. Wherefore the state of man after Adam's fall differs no more from the state of the same in pure naturals, than the despoiled differs from the naked: nor is human nature worse, if you take away original guilt, nor does it labor more with ignorance and infirmity, than it would be and labor if founded in pure naturals. Therefore the corruption of nature flowed not from the lack of some natural gift, nor from the accession of some bad quality, but from the sole loss of the supernatural gift on account of Adam's sin. Which opinion he proves to be common to the Scholastic Doctors old and more recent, with many testimonies of theirs afterwards brought forward.
pass_b_english: "Our opponents," Bellarmine says, "hold that the rectitude in which Adam was created was natural to him in this last sense, that is, as natural is opposed to supernatural. They hold it was a kind of health owed to nature and fitted to arise from nature itself when well formed, that is, uncorrupted. Men who lost that rectitude in Adam now lack some natural good, they say, as a beast would lack one if it were born blind, lame or feverish. And if original righteousness were now restored by God to some man, they would call it a supernatural gift by circumstance, not in itself, as we said of the eyes given back to the man born blind.

"We, however, hold that this rectitude, even in the lower part, was a supernatural gift, and supernatural in itself, not by circumstance, so that it neither flowed nor could flow from nature's principles. And because that gift was supernatural, as we shall prove shortly, once it was taken away human nature, left to itself, began to feel the conflict of lower part against higher that would have been natural, that is, would have followed from the condition of matter, had God not added the gift of righteousness to man.

"So man's state after Adam's fall differs from his state in a purely natural condition no more than a man stripped differs from a man naked. Take away original guilt, and human nature is no worse, and suffers no more from ignorance and weakness, than it would be and would suffer if it had been made in a purely natural condition. The corruption of nature, then, came not from the lack of some natural gift, nor from the addition of some bad quality, but solely from the loss of the supernatural gift because of Adam's sin."
Bellarmine then proves that this is the common view of the scholastic teachers, old and more recent, by citing many of their testimonies.
